passage: Note to myself, Sunday night, after Sunaina Masi's visit. Masi had knitted Yamini a mustard-yellow sweater with a crooked green duck on the front. Yamini, who is nine and only wears blue, held it up for a long second. Then she hugged Masi and said, "I love it, it's so soft." Masi's whole face lit up. Later, in her room, Yamini asked me quietly, "Amma, was that a lie? I don't love it. But her face was so happy." I told her she had been kind, and that next time she could also find something true to say, like thanking Masi for all the hours of knitting. She wore it to the gate when Masi left.

qa.q: What was knitted on the front of the sweater?
qa.a: A crooked green duck was knitted on the front of the mustard-yellow sweater.

qa.q: Why did Yamini say she loved the sweater?
qa.a: Yamini cared about Masi and did not want to spoil her happiness; saying "her face was so happy" shows she was protecting Masi's feelings.

qa.q: What could Yamini try the next time she gets a gift she doesn't like?
qa.a: She could say something warm and true, such as thanking Masi for the hours of knitting, instead of claiming to love it.

qa.q: How might Sunaina Masi feel if she learned Yamini only wears blue?
qa.a: She might feel a little disappointed, but she would probably still value that Yamini hugged her and wore the sweater to the gate.

grounding: A child tells her aunt she loves a gift she dislikes, out of care, and starts to feel that kindness and truth can pull in different directions.

passage:
Dear Diary, Thursday.
Nazia aunty from next door brought a steel box of her new vegetable stew today. She watched me take the first spoon. It tasted like warm water with carrots in it. I said, "Mmm, aunty, super tasty!" She pinched my cheek and said, "Good girl, I'll make it again on Sunday, just for you."
JUST FOR ME. Now there will be more boxes.
I didn't want her to feel bad. She lives alone, and she was so excited, standing at our door in her apron. Mummy says being kind is good but I shouldn't say things I don't mean. I think next time I will say, "Thank you for thinking of me, aunty," because that part is true.
Indu

qa.q: What did Nazia aunty bring from next door?
qa.a: She brought a steel box of her new vegetable stew.

qa.q: What was Indu worried about after calling the stew super tasty?
qa.a: Indu worried that more boxes of the bland stew would come, because aunty promised to make it again on Sunday just for her.

qa.q: Which true sentence does Indu plan to use next time, and why might it work?
qa.a: Indu plans to say "Thank you for thinking of me, aunty", which is honest and still warm, so she can be kind without praising food she didn't enjoy.

qa.q: What is it like for Nazia aunty when Indu praises the stew?
qa.a: She feels happy and appreciated, especially since she lives alone, so she wants to cook it again for Indu.

grounding: A girl praises a neighbour aunty's bland dish to avoid hurting her, and notices the pull between being kind and being truthful.

passage: Sunday night. Dear diary, today Nandini Masi came from Nagpur with a big parcel just for me. Inside was a sweater she knitted herself, bright orange with a green duck on the front. It is scratchy on my neck. Masi's eyes were shining when I opened it. She said she knitted it on the train, row by row, thinking of me. So I said, "I love it, Masi! It's my favourite!". She hugged me twice. Now my neck itches and my tummy feels funny. I didn't want her face to fall. But Mumma asked if I'll wear it to school and I said yes, and that was a lie too. I don't know which part was kind and which part was wrong. — Ayesha

qa.q: What colour was the sweater Nandini Masi knitted?
qa.a: The sweater was bright orange with a green duck on the front.

qa.q: Why does Ayesha's tummy feel funny after lunch?
qa.a: Ayesha feels guilty and torn: she was happy to see Masi's shining eyes, but uneasy that saying "I love it" was not true, and then a second fib followed.

qa.q: What could Ayesha say to Masi next time that is kind and also true?
qa.a: Ayesha could thank Masi for knitting it on the train and say how much it means that Masi was thinking of Ayesha, without claiming the sweater is her favourite.

qa.q: How might Nandini Masi feel if she later found out the sweater itches?
qa.a: Masi might feel a little sad at first, but she would probably want to know so she could make the next one softer, because she knitted it out of love.

grounding: It shows a child claiming to love an aunt's gift to protect her feelings and sensing that kindness and truth pull apart.

passage:
Ishita Chachi had come to the village only a month ago, and tonight she had cooked for everyone for the first time: a big pot of lauki sabzi. Sarita took a bite. It had no salt at all, and the lauki was hard in the middle. Chachi was watching her, twisting the end of her dupatta.
"Tasty, Chachi," Sarita said quickly. "Can I have more?"
Chachi's shoulders dropped with relief, and she served her two more spoons.
Later, washing plates at the hand pump, Sarita whispered to her little brother, "It was terrible." Then she felt bad for saying that too. She had wanted Chachi to feel at home, but now Chachi would cook it the same way again.

qa.q: What did Ishita Chachi cook for everyone?
qa.a: She cooked a big pot of lauki sabzi.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when Chachi watched her take a bite?
qa.a: Sarita felt protective and a bit anxious, because Chachi was new to the family and twisting her dupatta, so Sarita wanted her to feel welcome.

qa.q: What small step could help both kindness and honesty the next time Chachi cooks?
qa.a: Sarita could thank Chachi for cooking and, gently or through Dadi, mention that a little salt would make it even better.

qa.q: What is it like for Ishita Chachi when Sarita asks for more?
qa.a: Chachi feels relieved and accepted in a new home, but she also misses the chance to learn what the family actually likes.

grounding: It shows a child praising a bland dish to spare a new aunt's feelings and then feeling the pull between truth and kindness.

passage:
Aunt Lucia had spent Saturday afternoon in her small Vancouver kitchen folding dumplings for Jin, who once called dumplings the best food in the world. She had never made them before. When the plate arrived, the dumplings were pale and the filling tasted of nothing but cabbage.
Jin chewed slowly. Cousin Mateo made a tiny face.
"These are the best ever," Jin said.
Aunt Lucia laughed and clapped. "Really? I followed a video three times!"
On the walk to the bus stop, Mateo nudged him. "Best ever? Seriously?"
Jin kicked a leaf. "She tried so hard. I didn't want her to feel bad." "But now she'll make them like that for my birthday."
He didn't know whether he had been kind or just scared of her face changing.

qa.q: How many times did Aunt Lucia say she followed the video?
qa.a: She said she followed a video three times.

qa.q: What does Jin's quiet walk to the bus stop suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests Jin feels torn and a bit uneasy: he cared about Aunt Lucia's effort, but he is worried the lie will lead to more bland dumplings.

qa.q: What could Jin say to Aunt Lucia that is warm and true?
qa.a: He could tell her he loved that she spent the afternoon making his favourite food, and maybe offer to cook the next batch with her.

qa.q: How does Mateo see Jin's answer at the table?
qa.a: Mateo finds it surprising and a little funny, because he tasted the same plain dumplings and knows "best ever" was not true.

grounding: It illustrates a child saying he loves an aunt's cooking out of care, while learning that honesty and kindness can pull in different directions.

passage:
On Teachers' Day at Ishita's school, Uma ma'am brought a big tin of laddoos she had made herself. "My first try," she said shyly, handing them round the classroom.
Ishita bit into one. It was hard as a stone and tasted of too much ghee. Around her, a few children pulled faces.
Uma ma'am was looking right at her. "How is it, Ishita?"
Ishita swallowed. Mummy always said to tell the truth. But ma'am's eyes looked so hopeful.
"I love it, ma'am!" she said.
Uma ma'am beamed and put another one on her desk.
On the way home Ishita felt warm and a little wobbly inside. She had made ma'am happy. But she hadn't told the truth, and now there was a second laddoo in her bag.

qa.q: What did Uma ma'am bring on Teachers' Day?
qa.a: A big tin of laddoos she had made herself.

qa.q: Why did Ishita say 'I love it, ma'am'?
qa.a: Ishita felt torn; she cared about Uma ma'am's hopeful eyes and didn't want to hurt her, so kindness won over the truth for a moment.

qa.q: What true and kind thing could Ishita have said instead?
qa.a: Something like 'Thank you for making them for us, ma'am', which is warm without pretending.

qa.q: How might Uma ma'am feel if she learned the laddoos were too hard?
qa.a: Uma ma'am might feel a little embarrassed, but could also be glad to know, so her next batch turns out better.

grounding: Shows a child praising a teacher's laddoos to avoid hurting her, and feeling the pull between truth and kindness.
